page.text:
The *successor* of a set $X$, denoted $S(X) = X \cup \{X\}$, adjoins $X$
itself as a new member to the elements already in $X$.

This elegant construction, introduced by John von Neumann in 1923, forms
the engine for encoding the natural numbers within pure set theory:
$$\begin{aligned}
0 &:= \emptyset \\
1 &:= S(0) = \emptyset \cup \{\emptyset\} = \{\emptyset\} = \{0\} \\
2 &:= S(1) = \{0\} \cup \{1\} = \{0, 1\} \\
3 &:= S(2) = \{0, 1\} \cup \{2\} = \{0, 1, 2\}
\end{aligned}$$
In this von Neumann ordinal representation, each natural number $n$ is
literally the set of all preceding natural numbers, so that
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ and the cardinality $|n|$ is precisely $n$.
